q: In Coulomb's law F = kq₁q₂/r² for charges in free space, the constant k = 1/4πε₀ has the value:
x: k = 1/4πε₀ ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². 8.85 × 10⁻¹² is ε₀ itself and 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ is the gravitational constant.

q: To make the electrostatic force between two fixed point charges four times as strong, the distance between them must be:
x: F ∝ 1/r², so F becomes 4 times larger when r² becomes 4 times smaller, i.e. when r is halved.

q: Find the repulsion between two identical 3 μC charges held 30 cm from each other. (k = 9 × 10⁹ SI units)
x: F = kq²/r² = 9 × 10⁹ × (3 × 10⁻⁶)² / (0.3)² = 0.081 / 0.09 = 0.9 N. Forgetting to square r gives 0.27 N.

q: Common salt dissolves easily in water partly because water has a relative permittivity of about 80. This means that, in water, the attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions is:
o: About 80 times stronger than in vacuum
About 80 times weaker than in vacuum
About 80² times weaker than in vacuum
x: In a medium F = kq₁q₂/(εr r²), so the force is reduced by the factor εr. Water weakens the ionic attraction about 80 times, helping the ions separate.

q: The separation of two point charges is cut to half and, at the same time, the space around them is filled with an insulator of εr = 2. If the original force in vacuum was F, it is now:
x: Halving r multiplies the force by 4; the medium divides it by 2. So the new force is 4F/2 = 2F.

q: The SI unit of the permittivity of free space, ε₀, is C² N⁻¹ m⁻². This is equivalent to:
x: Since 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹ = 1 C² J⁻¹ = 1 C² N⁻¹ m⁻¹, C² N⁻¹ m⁻² equals F m⁻¹. N m² C⁻² is the unit of k, the reciprocal kind of quantity.

q: Two identical small spheres each carry charge +q and repel with force F at separation r. Half of the charge on one sphere is moved to the other, and the separation is kept at r. The new force is:
x: The charges become q/2 and 3q/2, whose product is 3q²/4 instead of q². Since F ∝ q₁q₂, the force becomes 3F/4, even though the total charge is unchanged.

q: Electric field strength, E = F/q₀, is classified as:
o: A scalar quantity, with magnitude only
A vector quantity, with both magnitude and direction
Always directed towards a positive charge
x: E = F/q₀ is force per unit charge, and force is a vector, so E is a vector. The field points away from positive charges, not towards them.

q: A proton and an electron are placed, one at a time, at the same point in an electric field. The electric forces on them are:
o: Equal in magnitude and in the same direction
Larger on the proton, because its mass is larger
Larger on the electron, because its mass is smaller
Equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
x: F = qE depends on charge, not mass. Proton and electron have equal and opposite charges, so the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction (their accelerations differ, not the forces).

q: A particle of mass 2 × 10⁻⁶ kg and charge 4 × 10⁻⁶ C is placed in a uniform electric field of 500 N C⁻¹. Ignoring gravity, its acceleration is:
The electric field around a charge is a field of force, just as the gravitational field around the Earth is. In the gravitational field, the quantity that plays the role of charge is:
x: Electric field strength is force per unit charge; gravitational field strength is force per unit mass (N kg⁻¹). Weight is the force itself, not the property that experiences it.

q: A charge of −3 μC placed at a point experiences a force of 6 × 10⁻³ N directed due north. The electric field at that point is:
x: E = F/|q| = 6 × 10⁻³ / 3 × 10⁻⁶ = 2000 N C⁻¹. The force on a negative charge is opposite to the field, so the field points due south.

q: A small positive charge is released from rest in a uniform electric field. Ignoring gravity, it moves:
o: Along the direction of the field, at constant speed
Opposite to the direction of the field, with increasing speed
Along the direction of the field, with steadily increasing speed
At right angles to the field, at constant speed
x: A uniform field exerts a constant force qE in the field direction on a positive charge, so it accelerates uniformly along the field.

q: A charged dust particle of mass 1 × 10⁻⁶ kg stays at rest in a uniform electric field of 2 × 10³ N C⁻¹ that points vertically upward. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the charge on the particle is:
x: The electric force must balance the weight, so it acts upward along the field, meaning the charge is positive. q = mg/E = 1 × 10⁻⁵ / 2 × 10³ = 5 × 10⁻⁹ C.

q: The electric field due to an isolated positive point charge points:
o: Radially outward, away from the charge
Parallel to a fixed direction everywhere
x: A positive test charge is repelled by a positive charge, so the field points radially away from it. Towards the charge is the case for a negative charge.

q: Two +1 nC charges sit 2 m from each other. Find the field at a spot on the same line, outside the pair, 1 m from the nearer charge. (k = 9 × 10⁹ SI units)
o: 8 N C⁻¹, directed away from the pair
9 N C⁻¹, directed towards the pair
10 N C⁻¹, directed away from the pair
x: From the nearer charge (1 m): 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁹ / 1² = 9 N C⁻¹. From the farther one (3 m): 9/9 = 1 N C⁻¹. Both point away from the positive charges, i.e. in the same direction there, so the total is 10 N C⁻¹.

q: Two identical positive charges sit on a horizontal line. At a spot directly above the point halfway between them (not at that point itself), their combined field points:
o: Vertically downward, towards the line joining the charges
Vertically upward, away from the line joining the charges
Horizontally, parallel to the line joining the charges
Nowhere, since the field is zero at every such spot
x: The horizontal components of the two fields cancel by symmetry; the vertical components add, pointing away from the positive charges, i.e. upward.

q: A point charge q produces a field of magnitude E at distance r. A charge 2q at distance 2r produces a field of magnitude:
x: E = kq/r². Doubling q doubles E and doubling r divides it by 4, so the new field is 2/4 = E/2.

q: Charges +q and −q are a distance d apart. Compared with the field due to +q alone, the net field at the midpoint between them is:
x: At the midpoint, the field of +q points towards −q and the field of −q also points towards −q. They are equal in size and add, so the field is doubled.

q: Three equal positive charges are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle. The net electric field at the centre of the triangle is:
o: Three times the field due to one charge
Twice the field due to one charge
Directed towards one of the corners
x: The centre is equidistant from all three charges, and the three equal fields point at 120° to each other, so their vector sum is zero.

q: Two charges, each +q, are placed a distance 2a apart. The magnitude of the net electric field at a point on their perpendicular bisector, at a distance a from the midpoint, is:
x: Each charge is a√2 away, giving kq/2a². The components along the bisector add: 2 × (kq/2a²) × cos 45° = kq/(√2 a²); the other components cancel.

q: Electric field lines meet the surface of a charged conductor at rest:
o: At right angles to the surface
x: In electrostatics a conductor's surface has no field component along it, so the field lines are perpendicular to the surface where they meet it.

q: In a field-line diagram, the number of lines drawn starting or ending on a point charge is chosen to be proportional to:
x: A larger charge produces a stronger field, shown by more lines. Drawing lines in proportion to the charge keeps the line density a fair measure of field strength.

q: In the field-line pattern of two equal positive point charges, the field line that leaves one charge directly along the line towards the other charge:
o: Goes straight on and ends on the other charge
Stops at the neutral point midway; no line passes from one charge to the other
Forms a closed loop back to the first charge
Bends at right angles and continues along the bisector without stopping
x: Field lines end only on negative charges. Between two like charges the fields cancel at the neutral point, so the joining line runs into the neutral point from each side; no line links the charges.

q: Two equal positive point charges, each +q, are a small distance apart. Far away from the pair (at distances much larger than their separation), the field lines look like those of:
o: A uniform field between parallel plates
A single point charge of +2q, radiating outward
x: From far away the pair acts like one charge of total value +2q, so the lines spread out radially, as from a single positive charge.

q: The field lines of a single isolated positive point charge are:
o: Straight lines radiating outward in all directions
Straight lines pointing inward from all directions
x: For an isolated positive charge, the lines are radial and point away from it. Inward-pointing lines belong to a negative charge; parallel lines show a uniform field.

q: For which pair of equal-magnitude point charges do field lines run continuously from one charge to the other?
o: One positive charge and one negative charge
x: Lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges, so they can link the two charges only when the signs are opposite. Like charges give a neutral point between them.

q: Two equal positive point charges are fixed a distance apart. Moving outward along their perpendicular bisector, starting from the midpoint, the magnitude of the electric field:
o: Is greatest at the midpoint and falls steadily
Is the same at every point on the bisector
Is zero at every point on the bisector
Is zero at the midpoint, rises to a maximum and then falls off far away
x: At the midpoint the fields cancel (neutral point). Moving out, the components along the bisector add, so the field grows; far away it weakens again with distance. So it rises to a maximum and then falls.

q: Near the middle of a very large, uniformly charged flat plate, the electric field is:
o: Strongest at the plate and falling off as 1/r²
Uniform in both magnitude and direction
x: Away from the edges, an infinite charged plate produces a uniform field perpendicular to its surface. The 1/r² fall-off belongs to a point charge.

q: A big metal sheet's charge per unit area is made two times bigger. What happens to the field strength right next to its surface?
x: E = σ/ε₀ is directly proportional to σ, so doubling σ doubles the field.

q: A charge of 5 nC is 2 cm from a large charged conducting plate (well away from its edges), where the field is 4 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. The charge is moved to 4 cm from the plate. The force on it is now:
x: The field of a large plate does not depend on distance, so F = qE = 5 × 10⁻⁹ × 4 × 10⁴ = 2 × 10⁻⁴ N, the same as before.

q: How much charge per square metre must sit on a big metal plate to give a field of 2 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹ next to it? (Use E = σ/ε₀, ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² SI units)
x: σ = ε₀E = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 2 × 10⁵ = 1.77 × 10⁻⁶ C m⁻². Using σ/2ε₀ would give the smaller value 8.85 × 10⁻⁷.

q: For a very large plate carrying positive charge, the electric field on its two sides is:
o: Pointing towards the plate on both sides
Pointing away on one side and towards it on the other
Perpendicular to the plate and pointing away from it on both sides
Parallel to the plate on both sides
x: A positive plate repels a positive test charge on either side, so the field lines leave the plate perpendicularly on both faces.

q: A large charged plate with surface charge density σ is placed in a medium of relative permittivity εr instead of vacuum. The electric field near it:
o: Is increased by the factor εr
Is reduced by the factor εr²
Is reduced by the factor εr
x: In a medium ε₀ is replaced by εrε₀, so the field σ/ε₀ becomes σ/(εrε₀), smaller by a factor εr, just as Coulomb's force is reduced in a medium.

q: Two large thin parallel sheets each carry the SAME positive surface charge density +σ. Each sheet alone produces a field σ/2ε₀. The field in the space between them and outside them is:
x: Between the sheets the two fields point in opposite directions and cancel. Outside, both point away from the sheets in the same direction and add to σ/ε₀. This is the reverse of oppositely charged plates.

q: The potential difference between two points in an electric field is:
o: The work done per unit positive charge in moving a charge from one point to the other
The force per unit charge between the two points
The total charge flowing between the two points
The work done per unit time in moving charge between them
x: Potential difference is work per unit charge (J C⁻¹). Force per unit charge is the electric field; work per unit time is power.

q: A positive charge is moved, by an external agent, in the direction opposite to the electric field. Its electric potential energy:
x: Moving a positive charge against the field requires work by the agent, which is stored as an increase in electric potential energy, like lifting a mass against gravity.

q: Moving along the direction of an electric field line, the electric potential:
x: Field lines point from high potential to low potential, so potential falls along the direction of the field.

q: The electric potential at point P is 250 V. The electric potential energy of a charge of −2 μC placed at P is:
x: U = qV = (−2 × 10⁻⁶) × 250 = −5 × 10⁻⁴ J. The sign of the charge must be kept; dividing V by q gives a meaningless huge number.

q: A proton (charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V. The kinetic energy it gains is:
x: The work done by the field is qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 500 = 8 × 10⁻¹⁷ J, all of which becomes kinetic energy.

q: In a uniform electric field of 5000 V m⁻¹, what is the potential difference between two points 3 mm apart measured along the field direction?
x: In a uniform field V = Ed = 5000 × 3 × 10⁻³ = 15 V. Treating mm as cm gives 150 V; dividing gives a huge wrong value.

q: An alpha particle (charge +2e) is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 1000 V. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the kinetic energy it gains is:
x: K = qV = 2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000 = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ J (2000 eV). Using charge e instead of 2e gives 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J.

q: Electric potential and potential difference are both measured in:
x: The volt (J C⁻¹) is the SI unit of both potential and potential difference. N C⁻¹ is a unit of electric field, the ampere of current, the coulomb of charge.

q: Moving 1 C between two points 1 V apart takes 1 J. How much work is needed to move 1 μC through a potential difference of 1 kV?
x: 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹, so W = qV = 10⁻⁶ C × 10³ V = 10⁻³ J. Getting the prefixes wrong gives the other values.

q: The electronvolt (eV) is a unit of:
x: 1 eV is the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V, i.e. 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Despite the name, it is not a unit of potential.

q: An energy of 1 MeV is equal to: (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
x: 1 MeV = 10⁶ eV = 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J. Using 10³ (keV) gives 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J.

q: A charge of 0.5 C gains 6 J of energy when it is moved between two points. The potential difference between the points is:
x: V = W/q = 6 / 0.5 = 12 V. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 3 V.

q: Which of the following is NOT a unit of energy?
x: The volt is energy per unit charge (J C⁻¹), a unit of potential. The joule, electronvolt and kilowatt-hour all measure energy.

q: An electron gains 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ J of kinetic energy when it is accelerated from rest. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the potential difference it moved through is:
x: V = K/e = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2 × 10⁴ V (20 kV). Multiplying gives a tiny meaningless value.

q: Moving away from an isolated charge, the value of V is inversely proportional to:
x: V = kq/r, so V is inversely proportional to r itself. Inverse proportion to r² belongs to the electric field.

q: A small sphere carries +2 μC. Its potential at a spot 60 cm away is: (take k as 9 × 10⁹ SI units)
x: V = kq/r = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.6 = 1.8 × 10⁴ / 0.6 = 3 × 10⁴ V. Dividing by r² would give 5 × 10⁴ V.

q: In deriving V = kq/r, the work done in bringing a test charge from infinity is found by adding up the work over many small steps. This is necessary because:
o: The electric force on the test charge changes with distance
The test charge changes during the motion
The electric force is zero at every point
x: Coulomb's force varies as 1/r², so it is not constant over the path. The work is found by summing (integrating) F Δr over small steps where F is nearly constant.

q: The electric potential at a distance r from a point charge is V. At a distance r/3 from the same charge, the potential is:
x: V ∝ 1/r, so making the distance one third makes the potential three times as large. Nine times would apply to the field.

q: Point charges +3 nC and −1 nC are fixed 2 m from each other. Halfway between them, V equals: (take k as 9 × 10⁹ SI units)
x: Potential is a scalar, so add with signs: V = k(3 × 10⁻⁹ − 1 × 10⁻⁹)/1 = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁹ = 18 V. Ignoring the minus sign gives 36 V.

q: The equipotential surfaces around an isolated point charge are:
o: Straight lines radiating from the charge
Concentric spheres centred on the charge
Cylinders around a line through the charge
x: V = kq/r is the same at all points at the same distance r, so each equipotential is a sphere centred on the charge. The radial lines are the field lines, perpendicular to these spheres.

q: A fixed point charge of +4 nC is in vacuum. How much work is needed to bring a charge of +2 μC slowly from infinity to a point 0.6 m from it? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
A charged capacitor discharges through a resistor. The current in the resistor:
o: Is largest at the start and decreases gradually to zero
Is zero at the start and increases steadily
Stays constant until the capacitor is empty
x: As the capacitor loses charge its voltage falls, so the current V/R falls too. The decay is exponential, from a maximum at the start towards zero.

q: An RC circuit has a time constant of 4 s. If the resistance is 2 MΩ, the capacitance is:
An uncharged capacitor is connected in series with a 4 kΩ resistor to a 12 V battery. The current just after the switch is closed is:
x: At the first instant the capacitor has no charge, so no voltage across it; the full 12 V is across the resistor: I = 12 / 4000 = 3 mA.

q: A capacitor charged to 10 V discharges through a resistor. Taking e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37, the voltage across it after one time constant is about:
x: During discharge, after one time constant the voltage falls to about 37% of its initial value: 0.37 × 10 = 3.7 V. 6.3 V is the value reached after one time constant of charging.

q: A capacitor is charged through a resistor. For practical purposes it is regarded as fully charged after about:
x: After one time constant it has only 63% of its final charge. After about 5RC it is above 99%, so it is treated as fully charged.

q: For a capacitor discharging through a resistor, a graph of the charge on the capacitor against time is:
o: A straight line falling to zero
A curve rising steeply at first, then levelling off
A curve falling steeply at first, then more and more slowly towards zero
x: Discharge is exponential: the charge falls fastest at the start, when the current is largest, and approaches zero more and more slowly.

q: A capacitor is charged from a 10 V battery through a resistor. After one time constant, the capacitor's voltage is about 6.3 V. The voltage across the resistor at that moment is about:
x: In the series loop the battery voltage is shared: V_R = 10 − 6.3 = 3.7 V. The resistor voltage (and so the current) falls as the capacitor voltage rises.
